narrative:
The model predicted a 54% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 25.5, it sits well below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the skills the bar exam tests most heavily.

Your undergraduate GPA came next in importance but worked in the opposite direction. The 2.8 GPA actually pulled the prediction slightly toward passing, though not enough to overcome the other factors.

Your third-year class ranking was the third most influential element and again pushed toward failure. Placing in the 3rd decile is noticeably lower than the average 5.8 decile seen among accepted students, indicating that your performance in law school itself raised concerns about readiness for the bar.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through intensive preparation, as this carries the greatest weight. Consider retaking the test and reapplying once you can demonstrate stronger performance in that key area.
